concept.title: Shopping for Components
concept.shortdesc: How to determine what component models and specifications will your desktop build use

conbody.p: Now that you have a strong idea of what you want out of your build project it’s time to start looking at what components are available. There are several sites that help group together parts into general performance tiers, such as Logical Increments, but it’s important to take any rating as a suggestion and do your own follow up research, especially if you’re looking at a larger build budget. It’s worth repeating that computer components can be a volatile industry, and new technology, geopolitical shifts, and consumer trends can have an enormous impact in a short period of time.

One of the most popular resources is PCPartPicker, a site that compiles information on computer part pricing and reviews and has robust planning tools. The most useful tool is the Builder, which allows you to select parts from a sortable list and add them to your shopping list. The site does not sell parts directly, so adding a part to your list will generate an affiliate link to the current least expensive supplier. As you add items to your list future items can be filtered by compatibility using an option on the left side of the screen (on by default). This ensures parts are at least advertised to work together, although physical dimensions aren’t checked. As you fill out your shopping list, the site automatically generates a link you can save or share with others.

Computer building is a popular hobby and there are several online forums, including PCPartPicker’s own forum, who gladly will discuss your choices in detail and at great length. More in-depth reviews of parts can be found online. Some reputable sites for reviews are AnandTech, TechPowerUp, and TechSpot.

In general, I would recommend never buying a used PSU, and being very cautious about buying a used GPU. GPUs are often used in bulk for continuous repetitive tasks, like cryptography, and then swapped out and sold used when new technology becomes cost effective. A used GPU, even a very recent one, may have been working 24 hours a day, 7 days a week for months before being resold. It may have a deceptive amount of wear and tear with a significantly shortened life. Other components are fine to buy used if you can find a good discount from a reputable seller.
